segments.source: A parent is one generation above a child. A grandparent is two parent-links above. People who share a parent are siblings under this simplified model. For the cross-domain check, independent reports = total reports − duplicate copies. For this verification, the final number of sheets equals starting sheets plus received sheets.
Task.

What family relation between Lina and Sara follows from the stated links? Cross-domain check: how many non-duplicate reports remain? Mixed-domain verification: how many sheets are available after the delivery?
Step-by-step solution.

1. Noah and Owen are siblings because they share parent Maya. 2. Lina is child of Noah; Sara is child of Owen. 3. Children of siblings are cousins in this model. Cross-domain check: 11−4=7 independent reports remain. Mixed-domain verification: 95+6=101.
Answer.
Lina and Sara are cousins under the implied family tree. Cross-domain answer: 7 independent reports. Mixed-domain answer: 101 map sheets.
Knowledge takeaway.
Family relations can be derived step by step from a small set of explicit links.
Formal model.
Directed parent graph; kinship predicates derived from path length and shared ancestors.
N13. Anachronisms and temporal compatibility
Problem 936. Temporal compatibility in a story set in 1400
Knowledge context.
Anachronism can be tested as a compatibility problem when the relevant date ranges are supplied.
Given facts.

For this problem, availability intervals are: Technology A: 1200–1600; Institution B: 1500–1900; Tool C: 1700–2000; Practice D: 1300–1450. A story is set in 1400 and mentions Technology A and Tool C together. Cross-domain check: on a field sketch, 1 cm represents 3 km and two checkpoints are 7 cm apart.
Rules.

An item is temporally compatible with a year only if the year lies inside its stated availability interval. An anachronism is an item placed outside its given interval. For the cross-domain check, real distance = sketch distance × kilometres per centimetre.
Task.
Which mentioned item, if any, is anachronistic in the story? Cross-domain check: what real distance separates the checkpoints?
Step-by-step solution.
1. Check 1400 against Technology A interval 1200–1600. 2. Check 1400 against Tool C interval 1700–2000. 3. Items outside their intervals: ['Tool C']. Cross-domain check: 7×3=21 km.
Answer.
Anachronistic: Tool C. Cross-domain answer: 21 km.
Knowledge takeaway.
The reasoning does not require memorizing invention dates if the intervals are part of the problem.
Formal model.
Interval membership test for each object-event pair.

N14. Provenance and chain of custody
Problem 941. Provenance and chain of custody: case 1
Knowledge context.
Provenance records where an object came from and how it moved between custodians.
Given facts.

An artifact record states: found by Excavator on day 1; transferred to Museum A on day 2; sent from Museum A to Research Lab on day 5; returned by Research Lab to Museum B on day 8. Every transfer must name both sender and receiver. Cross-domain check: a survey team starts work at 12:00 and works for 2 hour(s) without a break. Mixed-domain verification: a regional archive has 96 map sheets and receives 2 additional sheets during the exercise.
Rules.

A continuous chain of custody requires each handoff to connect the previous holder to the next. A missing sender or receiver creates a gap that limits certainty about continuous custody. For the cross-domain check, finishing time = starting time + duration. For this verification, the final number of sheets equals starting sheets plus received sheets.
Task.

Is the stated chain of custody complete under the rule? If not, identify the gap. Cross-domain check: at what time does the team finish? Mixed-domain verification: how many sheets are available after the delivery?
Step-by-step solution.

1. Read the transfers in time order. 2. Check that every transfer links the previous holder to the next. 3. Every handoff names both sides and connects continuously. Cross-domain check: 12+2=14, so the team finishes at 14:00. Mixed-domain verification: 96+2=98.
Answer.
The chain is complete under the stated rule. Cross-domain answer: 14:00. Mixed-domain answer: 98 map sheets.
Knowledge takeaway.
A strong provenance claim depends on an unbroken sequence of documented handoffs.
Formal model.
Time-ordered path through holders; verify continuity of sender/receiver pairs.
Problem 942. Provenance and chain of custody: case 2
Knowledge context.

Given facts.

An artifact record states: found by Excavator on day 1; transferred to Museum A on day 2; sent from Museum A to Research Lab on day 5; returned by Research Lab to Museum B on day 8. Every transfer must name both sender and receiver. The record for day 5 names Research Lab as receiver but does not name the sender. Cross-domain check: a local committee has 14 members, requires at least 8 present for quorum, and 14 are present.
Rules.

A continuous chain of custody requires each handoff to connect the previous holder to the next. A missing sender or receiver creates a gap that limits certainty about continuous custody. For the cross-domain check, quorum exists when present members ≥ the stated threshold.
Task.
Is the stated chain of custody complete under the rule? If not, identify the gap. Cross-domain check: is quorum met?
Step-by-step solution.

1. Read the transfers in time order. 2. Check that every transfer links the previous holder to the next. 3. The day-5 record lacks a sender, so the chain has a gap. Cross-domain check: compare 14 with 8; 14≥8 is true.
Answer.
The chain is incomplete because the day-5 sender is missing. Cross-domain answer: quorum is met.
Knowledge takeaway.
A strong provenance claim depends on an unbroken sequence of documented handoffs.
Formal model.
Time-ordered path through holders; verify continuity of sender/receiver pairs.
